title: 1 Corinthians 9:15–23
context: Paul now explains why he refuses the support he has just proven he may claim. Preaching itself is a necessity laid on him, so his only reward is to offer the gospel free of charge. From there he states a broader rule of his ministry: though free from all, he has made himself a servant to all, becoming like Jews, like those under the law, like those outside the law, and like the weak, so that by all means he might save some. Arminian readers often find in verse 22 a strong statement of genuine human means in salvation. Reformed readers agree that the means are real but place them under God’s sovereign purpose to save his people.

verses.text: But I have used none of these things, and I don’t write these things that it may be done so in my case; for I would rather die, than that anyone should make my boasting void.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul has used none of these rights and is not writing to get them now; he would rather die than lose his boast. Arminian readers see the freedom of a minister who serves out of love rather than obligation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Paul’s boast is not in himself but in a ministry kept free from any appearance of self-interest. His aim is that Christ alone, not the preacher, be honored.

verses.text: For if I preach the Good News, I have nothing to boast about; for necessity is laid on me; but woe is to me, if I don’t preach the Good News.
verses.arminianNotes: Preaching is no grounds for boasting, for necessity is laid on him; woe to him if he does not preach. Arminian readers see a calling that Paul could resist, which is why he speaks of woe for disobedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the compulsion of a divine call. Paul was laid hold of by Christ, and the necessity he feels reflects God’s sovereign appointment of him to this work.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions take Paul’s call as compelling. Arminian readers stress the real accountability implied by “woe.” Reformed readers stress the divine necessity laid on him by God’s appointment.

verses.text: For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward. But if not of my own will, I have a stewardship entrusted to me.
verses.arminianNotes: If he preaches willingly he has a reward; if not, he is still entrusted with a stewardship. Arminian readers see a distinction between Paul’s free choices and his duty, which both matter to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Paul as a steward who must be faithful regardless of his feelings. The stewardship comes from God, and faithfulness is its measure, as Paul said in 4:2.

verses.text: What then is my reward? That, when I preach the Good News, I may present the Good News of Christ without charge, so as not to abuse my authority in the Good News.
verses.arminianNotes: His reward is to make the gospel free of charge, so as not to use his full right. Arminian readers see Paul’s joy in offering grace as freely as he received it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a fitting match between the message and its delivery. A gospel of free grace is commended when it is preached without charge.

verses.text: For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.
verses.arminianNotes: Though free from all, Paul made himself a servant to all, so that he might gain the more. Arminian readers see Paul’s whole strategy aimed at persuading as many people as possible, which assumes that people can truly respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that Paul labors to gain many. They see no tension between God’s election and this effort, since God has ordained the means of preaching as well as its result.

verses.text: To the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain those who are under the law;
verses.arminianNotes: To the Jews he became as a Jew, and to those under the law as under the law, though not himself under the law. Arminian readers see flexible, culturally sensitive mission aimed at winning hearers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see liberty used in love. Paul could keep Jewish customs without making them a condition of salvation, which guards the gospel of grace while removing needless offense.

verses.text: to those who are without law, as without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might win those who are without law.
verses.arminianNotes: To those without law he became as without law, yet not without law to God but under the law of Christ. Arminian readers see freedom that remains accountable to Christ’s commands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in “the law of Christ” support for the moral law as a continuing rule of life for believers. Calvin called this the third and principal use of the law, guiding those already justified.

verses.text: To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some.
verses.arminianNotes: To the weak he became weak; he has become all things to all people, that by all means he might save some. Arminian readers see this as strong evidence that human means matter in salvation, and that the outcome of preaching is not fixed apart from them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Paul as God’s instrument. He says “save some,” not all, and Reformed interpreters see God working through Paul’s adaptable labors to save those he has chosen.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readers read “by all means… save some” as showing that real human effort affects who is saved. Reformed readers read it as describing the God-ordained means by which the elect are surely brought to faith.

verses.text: Now I do this for the sake of the Good News, that I may be a joint partaker of it.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul does all this for the gospel’s sake, that he may share in it with them. Arminian readers note that Paul seems to see his own participation in the gospel’s blessings as something he must pursue, which leads into the warning of verses 24–27.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Paul’s desire to be a fellow partaker as the natural longing of a believer. His labors flow from his share in the gospel rather than earning it.
